title: Efficiency Effectiveness and Equity in Health Financing
path: Health Care Financing and Insurance Scheme

headings.title: Introduction to Health Financing Core Concepts
headings.content:
Health financing is the function of a health system that deals with the mobilization, accumulation, and allocation of money to cover the health needs of the population. A well-functioning health financing system aims to make services available, accessible, and affordable to everyone while protecting households from catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditures. Within public health frameworks, money is collected through various revenue streams—such as general taxation, mandatory social health insurance, voluntary private insurance, and direct out-of-pocket payments by patients at the point of care. 

Direct out-of-pocket spending remains a dominant mechanism in many low- and middle-income countries, frequently driving vulnerable families into poverty when severe illness strikes. To counteract this, modern health sector reforms emphasize prepaid pooling mechanisms, where financial risks are shared across a broad population base. Understanding how funds flow from revenue collection to purchasing health services forms the foundational basis for analyzing health system performance. Without structured financial tracking, health institutions struggle to maintain basic commodities, leading to severe supply chain breakdowns and compromised patient care outcomes.

headings.title: Defining Efficiency in Health Care Financing
headings.content: Efficiency in health care refers to maximizing the health outcomes derived from a given set of financial and physical resources. Resources in any healthcare delivery system—ranging from skilled nursing personnel and diagnostic machinery to essential medicines—are inherently scarce. When resources are wasted through administrative bloat, corruption, or poor supply chain management, fewer patients receive the care they require. Financial efficiency demands that the relationship between inputs (money, staff, time) and outputs (treatments delivered, immunizations administered) is optimized so that no waste occurs.

headings.title: Allocative Versus Technical Efficiency
headings.content:
Health sector analysts divide efficiency into two distinct categories to pinpoint where financial systems succeed or fail:

- **Allocative efficiency**: Occurs when society's scarce resources are distributed among different health programs or interventions to maximize overall population health. For example, shifting funds from expensive urban tertiary care toward primary health care immunizations often yields greater overall community health returns.
- **Technical efficiency**: Achieved when a specific health intervention or service is produced at the absolute lowest possible cost without sacrificing quality. This involves streamlining nursing workflows, preventing drug wastage in hospital pharmacies, and maintaining equipment properly to avoid premature replacement.

headings.title: Understanding Effectiveness in Health Interventions
headings.content: While efficiency measures the cost-to-output ratio, effectiveness examines whether a health intervention actually produces the desired beneficial outcome in real-world clinical practice. An intervention can be technically efficient—delivered cheaply and quickly—yet completely ineffective if it targets the wrong pathology or relies on outdated medical guidelines. Effectiveness looks beyond laboratory trials to evaluate how treatments perform when administered by general nurses and physicians working within standard, often imperfect, healthcare environments.

headings.title: Ensuring Equity in Health Care Access and Financing
headings.content: Equity implies fairness in the distribution of health care services and financial contributions across a population. In health financing, equity has two primary pillars: equal access for equal need, and financing according to ability to pay rather than disease risk or social status. When health systems rely heavily on out-of-pocket user fees, equity collapses because impoverished individuals cannot afford basic care while wealthier citizens can easily pay for advanced treatments. Achieving equity requires targeted subsidies, progressive taxation, and robust social health insurance schemes that protect marginalized populations from medical destitution.

headings.title: Horizontal Versus Vertical Equity in Resource Allocation
headings.content:
Equity in health resource distribution is further divided into two operational concepts:

- **Horizontal equity**: Demands that individuals with the exact same health care needs receive equal treatment and utilization of services, regardless of their income, gender, or ethnicity. For example, two pregnant women presenting with identical high-risk obstetric complications should receive the same standard of emergency nursing care.
- **Vertical equity**: Requires that individuals with greater health needs or lower socioeconomic status receive preferential treatment or additional resources to bridge health disparities. For instance, allocating extra mobile immunization clinics and subsidized nutritional supplements to remote, impoverished rural settlements exemplifies vertical equity in action.

headings.title: Balancing Efficiency, Effectiveness, and Equity in Nigeria's Health System
headings.content: Balancing efficiency, effectiveness, and equity represents a complex policy challenge within Nigeria's pluralistic health sector. Federal and state health agencies constantly grapple with constrained budgets, underfunded primary healthcare centers, and heavy reliance on out-of-pocket spending by citizens. While striving for technical and allocative efficiency is necessary to stretch limited government funds, policymakers must ensure that cost-cutting measures do not compromise the clinical effectiveness of treatments or widen equity gaps for vulnerable rural populations. Strengthening the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) and expanding state-level health insurance schemes are critical steps toward harmonizing these three pillars, ensuring that financial protection reaches the most underserved Nigerians.
